o: Keys are single uppercase letters, values are at most 8 chars possibly containing %KEY% placeholders, and dependencies are acyclic. Example 2 shows nesting: %C% expands to abc%B%, which then expands to abcace. With ≤10 keys and tiny strings, almost anything works; the clean solutions are memoized DFS (expand each key once) or iterative fixpoint substitution (always expand the leftmost placeholder until none remain).
k: Acyclicity guarantees both memoized recursion and fixpoint iteration terminate.
Memoize resolved key values so each key's value is expanded exactly once.
Scanning for the leftmost '%...%' and splicing in the raw value works because unresolved parts get expanded in later passes.

a.i: resolve(key) walks its value, replacing each placeholder with resolve(inner). A memo map ensures each key is fully expanded once; the text itself is expanded the same way.
s: resolve(key): scan its value; splice resolve(inner) for each %inner%.
Expand the text with the same scanner.
a.t: O(total expanded length) — each key resolved once, strings are tiny

a.i: Repeatedly find the first %k% in the text and splice in the raw value of k. Any placeholders inside the spliced value will be expanded by subsequent iterations; the DAG guarantee ensures progress, so the loop terminates with no '%' left.
s: While text contains '%': locate the first pair and replace with mp[key].
a.t: O(L²) worst case for text length L — each pass expands one placeholder; trivial here

w: Either approach is fine at these constraints; memoized DFS generalizes better (larger inputs, shared subexpressions), fixpoint splicing is the least code. Pitfall: assuming values contain no nested placeholders, or mishandling adjacent placeholders like %A%%B%. Follow-up: detect and report cycles instead of relying on the guarantee.
